course.title: Spleen
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Located in left upper quadrant, between fundus of stomach and diaphragm, protected by lower portion of rib cage
  • Covered by peritoneum and splenic capsule → give rise to splenic trabeculae carrying arteries and veins
  • 12 cm long
  • Position maintained by several ligaments a. Spleno-phrenic b. Spleno-renal c. Spleno-colic d. Gastro-splenic – short gastric artery
  • Celiac artery - Splenic artery - 4-5 segmental trabecular arteries - arterial capillaries - red pulp venous sinuses &

reticular tissue

  • Venous sinuses - pulp trabecular veins - splenic vein - portal vein
  • Innervation - sympathetic nerve fibers from celiac plexus, left vagus nerve
  • Accessory spleens in 14-30%, usually seen at hilum, greater omentum, ligaments of spleen

Structure

  • 3 zones of pulp

a. White pulp – splenic parenchyma consisting of lymphoreticular tissue (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells) b. Red pulp – splenic parenchyma consisting of reticular tissue (cord, sinuses), blood vessels, blood cellular elements c. Marginal zone – poorly defined vascular space between pulps; contains sequestered foreign material, plasma and abnormal cellular elements

White pulpRed pulp
= circular structure made mainly of lymphocytes
- similar to nodules of lymph node		- surrounds white pulp and contains mainly red blood cells
and macrophages
- phagocytize old red blood cells

Physiology

A. Filtering- Splenic blood flow → 350 ml/day
- Monitors and manages blood cells and immune functions
- During fetal development, spleen produces red and white blood cells
- Red cells that pass-through spleen undergo “cleaning” or repair
- Abnormal and old red cells and platelets are destroyed
- Cleans also germs, antigens and cellular debris
B. Immunologic
function		1. Opsonin production (essential in protection against pathogenic bacteria)
2. Antibody and lymphokines synthesis for complement system (IgM)
3. Protection from infection (promotes phagocytosis and destruction of bacteria)
C. Storage
function		- Storage of red blood cells, lymphocytes and other formed elements
1. Platelets → 1/3 are stored in spleen
2. In splenomegaly, up to 80% of platelets may be stored in spleen → thrombocytopenia
D. Hematopoietic
function		- Lymphoid hematopoiesis (but not primary site)
- By 5. month of gestation, spleen no longer has hematopoietic function but retains
capacity throughout life
E. Circulatory
function		- Provides aortic and portal blood flow dynamics

Clinical diagnosis

  • 1. History
  • Bleeding disorders, anemic syndromes, recurrent infections, abdominal trauma
  • 2. Symptoms
  • Often asymptomatic
  • Discomfort or LUQ pain, with/ without being referred to left shoulder (violent pain attributed to splenic infarction/

abscess)

  • Hemolytic jaundice - acholic stools, coluric urine, lack of itching
  • 3. Physical exam
  • Normally not palpable
  • Felt in 2% of healthy asthenic adults
  • Deep inspiration, pat. in supine or right lateral position, hand under left costal margin
  • Movement during inspiration and expiration
  • Felt in splenomegaly
  • No significant dullness elicited by percussion over spleen
  • In splenomegaly → dullness detected at 9th ICS in left anterior axillary line
  • 4. Imaging
  • US – method of choice, size, collections, hematoma or splenic tumors, splenic ruptures, differential diagnosis to

other abdominal tumors

  • Doppler US - traumatic emergencies
  • CT - tumor and traumatic spleen
  • MRI - less useful
  • - 99 Tc colloid - scanning of reticuloendothelial system (RES), splenoportal axis
  • 5. Laboratory examination
  • Blood cytology mandatory for peripheral cytopenia: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, anemia
  • Blood cytology in bone marrow in hypersplenism
  • Immunological examinations: direct and indirect Coombs test, autoantibody tests

Hypersplenism

= Splenomegaly → exacerbation of normal splenic function → spleen rapidly and prematurely destroy blood cells

  • Reduction in number of RBC, WBC, platelets
  • Compensatory rise in production in bone marrow → reticulocytosis
  • Recurring fever and infection
  • Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
Primary hypersplenismSecondary hypersplenism
- Diagnosis by exclusion
- Congenital hemolytic anemia
- Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Splenic neutropenia
- Immune hemolytic anemia
- Responds to splenectomy
- Steroids do not improve condition		- Portal hypertension → splenic congestion
- Lymphoma, Chronic leukemia
- Chronic bacterial infections: tuberculosis, syphilis
- RA, SLE, sarcoidosis
- Thesaurismosis: Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick d.
- Does not warrant splenectomy

DD of splenomegaly → tumors in left upper quadrant

  • Abdominal wall tumors
  • Retroperitoneal sarcomas
  • Left adrenal tumors
  • Left kidney tumors
  • Left hydronephrosis
  • Cancer of tail of pancreas
  • Cancer of greater curvature
  • Giant tumors in vicinity
  • Hypertrophy of left hepatic lobe

Splenic rupture

  • Very fragile → most affected by abdominal trauma
  • Especially in splenomegaly
  • Disruption of spleen’s parenchyma, capsule, blood supply

Etiology

  • Blunt trauma → spleen contusion, ruptured spleen (immediate rupture, delayed rupture)
  • Penetrating wounds (cold weapons or firearms)
  • Iatrogenic injury (intra-operatory during colon, stomach and pancreatic surgery)
  • Spontaneous rupture → hematologic disorders

Pathology

  • Bleeding → limited (hematoma) or hemoperitoneum
  • Subcapsular splenic hematoma - after blunt trauma, preserved capsule integrity, maybe secondary capsule rupture and delayed hemorrhage, seclusion, abscess or resorption
  • Perisplenic hematoma - capsular effraction, trauma or secondary to subcapsular hematoma, requires careful monitoring under conservative treatment, maybe secondary rupture, c
  • Splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum - mainly on convex side of spleen, can be fatal, splenic pedicle avulsion is very rare
  • Wounds produced by cold weapons - usually avoid hilum, with/ without detachment of parenchymal fragments, firearm can cause "spleen explosion"
    • a) Splenic rupture
    • Intraperitoneal
    • 90% of blunt trauma
    • b) Delayed rupture
    • Interval of days or weeks between injury and bleeding (10-15%)
    • Quiescent period for < 7 days up to 2 weeks
    • Related to temporary tamponade of minor lacerations or slowly enlarging subcapsular hematoma
    • c) Occult splenic rupture
    • Pseudocyst of spleen (1%)

Clinical manifestation

  • Hypovolemia/ hypovolemic shock (anxiety, thirst, faintness, severe skin paleness, cold and wet hands/feet,

hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria

  • Localized (LUQ) or generalized abdominal pain
  • Kehr’s sign = pain at tip of left shoulder → phrenic nerve transports diaphragmatic irritation
  • With/ without signs of peritoneal irritation
  • Superficial thrombophlebitis
  • Hemoperitoneum → abdominal distension, shifting dullness to percussion in left flank/ LUQ (Ballance’s sign),

paralytic ileus, bulging of Pouch of Douglas

Investigations

Lab- CBC → serial Hct determination, anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis
US- Splenic hematoma or hemoperitoneum
Abdominal X-ray- Fractured ribs
- Elevated immobile diaphragm
- Enlarged splenic shadow
- Medial displacement of gastric shadow
- Widening shadow between splenic flexure and preperitoneal fat
CT scan
Angiography

Treatment → surgery

  • 1) Regaining vital functions
  • 2) Non-surgical spleen preservation in carefully selected cases (hemodynamically stable, splenic injury without active bleeding, absence of associated lesions), hospitalization for 6-8 days with continuous clinical monitoring and imaging
  • 3) Spleen-preserving surgery (capsular suture, tissue adhesives, argon plasma coagulation)
  • 4) Complete splenectomy in total spleen damage or splenic bleeding that cannot be stopped

Spleen laceration

  • Extending from top diagonally across to bottom of specimen, is a large tear in capsule of

spleen, exposing pulp

  • Splenic lacerations are common in automobile accidents and are common if spleen has

undergone enlargement due to some reason

Splenic abscess

  • Rare purulent collections caused by bacteria or fungi
  • Infection of trasplenic hematoma or necrotic lesion, hematogenic contamination of splenic infarction
  • Hematogenic spread from primary extrasplenic focus: endocarditis, lung abscess, osteomyelitis, typhoid fever
  • Lymphatic spread from neighboring organs: pancreatic suppuration, left colic tumors
  • Risk factors - systemic infections, multiple trauma or immunosuppressed
  • Sudden occurrence of LUQ pain, tenderness during palpation, superficial thrombophlebitis, fever, malaise
  • Laboratory tests - leukocytosis, positive blood cultures
  • Ultrasound - fist choice, irregular hypoechoic with echoes inside
  • CT scan confirms
  • Treatment - antibiotherapy + surgery → splenectomy or ultrasound-guided percutaneous abscess drainage

Splenic hydatid cyst

  • 3rd most frequency after lungs and liver
  • Single or multiple, varying in diameter, clear or purulent content
  • May cause compression of neighboring organs
  • Perisplenitis, adhering to neighboring organs, splenic rupture, splenic calcification (rare)
  • Splenomegaly
  • Free rupture produces anaphylactic shock and splenic abscess
  • Ultrasound-based diagnosis + positive serological tests: Casoni test, indirect hemagglutination test, ELISA
  • Surgical treatment: partial cyst resection, partial splenectomy (after evacuation by aspiration and inactivation with scolicidal agents), total splenectomy

Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)

  • Characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytes
  • Most patients are young
  • Clinical symptoms are similar to those of a severe upper respiratory tract infection
  • Spleen is enlarged and palpable in > 50%
  • Splenic rupture may occur

Vascular pathologies

Splenic vein thrombosis

  • Massive splenomegaly
  • Thrombosis secondary to pancreatitis
  • Associated with esophageal varices (without hepatic damage)
  • Cured by splenectomy
  • Diagnosis → Eco-Doppler, CT and angiography
  • Main causes: acute or chronic pancreatitis, pseudocysts, trauma, splenic vein abnormalities
  • Other causes: neoplasms (leukemia, lymphoma, metastatic CA), myeloproliferative disorders, increase in RBC destruction (thalassemia major), disorders in immune response (infectious mononucleosis), diseases that infiltrate spleen (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis)

Splenic artery aneurysm

  • Frequently in women
  • Atheromatous, destruction of tunica media, trauma, syphilis, pancreatitis or malformative
  • Mostly asymptomatic
  • LUQ pain, referred into left subscapular area, exacerbated by physical effort
  • Rupture and signs of hypovolemic shock
  • Radiologic examinations (doppler, angiography) - calcified splenic artery and dilation
  • Treatment - emergency surgery, aneurysmal sac resection and splenic artery ligation, vascular prosthesis or vascular anastomosis, splenectomy, splenopancreatectomy

Splenic arteriovenous fistulas

  • Due to aneurysms, trauma, splenectomy, inflammatory pancreatic diseases
  • Symptoms - colicky abdominal pain, splenomegaly, portal hypertension (hyperinflux), heavy breath in spleen area during auscultation
  • Diagnosis by selective arteriography
  • Treatment - vein ligation and resection of arterio-venous communication or splenectomy

Splenic infarction

  • Causes - embolic (valvular heart disease, endocarditis, myocardial infarction, aneurysms) or systemic (sickle- cell anemia, chronic myelogenous leukemia, polycythemia vera, lymphomas, osteomyelofibrosis, polyarteritisnodosa, sepsis)
  • Progression - pseudocysts, abscess, retractile fibrosis
  • Diagnosis - ultrasound or angiography
  • Splenectomy

Lysosomal storage diseases

Gaucher’s disease

  • = Inherited disorder of lipid metabolism → result in massive splenomegaly and hypersplenism
  • Accumulation of glucocerebroside in monocytophagocytic system
  • Jewish population
  • Hepatomegaly with hepatic fibrosis → portal hypertension
  • Splenectomy does not cure but remits symptoms and corrects blood cytopenia
  • Bone marrow transplantation

Niemann-Pick disease

  • Sphingomyelinase deficiency → accumulation of sphingomyelin in macrophages in spleen, liver, lymph nodes, central nervous system and bone marrow
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Splenectomy to reduce symptoms, but it does not influence disease progression

Hereditary and Hematological disorders

Hereditary spherocytosis

  • Autosomal dominant → membrane defects resulting in reduced surface (spherocytes) → not being able to cross inter-endothelial holes → being retained in red pulp cords → destroyed
  • Increased osmotic fragility of erythrocytes → anemia, acholuric jaundice occuring in episodes, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones
  • Hemolytic crises (impaired general condition, tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain)
  • Lab tests: anemia, reticulocytosis, microspherocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, increased urobilinogen, Coomb's negative
  • Imaging: US, skull X ray "tower-like" skull
  • Treatment: splenectomy after age of 6 years, failure when accessory spleens not discovered

Hereditary elliptocytosis

  • Presence of ovalocytes (erythrocyte cell membrane abnormality)
  • Clinically – asymptomatic, hemolysis, splenomegaly
  • Splenectomy in severe hemolysis

Sickle-cell disease

  • “sickle-shaped” red blood cells containing HgS
  • Clinically - painful hemolytic crisis, vascular occlusive events
  • Splenectomy necessary due to high risk of splenic infarction

Thalassemia

  • Congenital anemia characterized by deficient synthesis of one or more hemoglobin polypeptide chains
  • Homozygous - thalassemia major and heterozygous - thalassemia minor
  • First year of life, progressive anemia, hemolytic jaundice, splenomegaly, delayed bone growth and bone loss
  • Hypochromic microcytic anemia, “target-shaped” red blood cells, indirect hyperbilirubinemia
  • Splenectomy

Splenic neutropenia

  • Splenomegaly, peripheral neutropenia and normal/hyperplastic bone marrow
  • Histiocytic granulocytes in spleen → excessive intraspleniclysis
  • LUQ pain, splenomegaly and recurrent infections
  • Splenectomy

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

  • Abnormal production of antibodies
  • Splenic macrophages and Kupffer cells capture erythrocytes that are attached to autoantibodies
  • Onset after 40 years, chronic hemolytic anemia, fluctuating jaundice, splenomegaly
  • Anemia, presence of spherocytes and microspherocytes, reticulocytosis and erythroid hyperplasia
  • Immunosuppressive medication, blood transfusion, splenectomy

Felty’s syndrome

  • Syndrome consisting of severe rheumatoid arthritis, granulocytopenia and splenomegaly
  • Severe, persistent and recurrent infections
  • Moderate splenomegaly
  • Splenectomy

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

  • Young women without medical history
  • Sometimes in systemic lupus erythematosus, Hodgkin's disease, AIDS
  • Hemorrhagiparous syndrome, peripheral thrombocytopenia, bone marrow megakaryocytes, antiplatelet antibodies
  • Petechiaeon slopeor compression areas (bone prominences), gingival bleeding, epistaxis, bruising, uterine bleeding, hematuria, intracranial haemorrhage
  • Spleen normal sized
  • Corticotherapy, splenectomy

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

  • Severe prognosis
  • Disseminated obstructions in arterioles and capillaries caused by platelet microthrombi
  • Hemolytic anemia, jaundice, purpura, menometroragy, neurospihic syndrome (aphasia, emiparesis, delirium, seizures)
  • Corticosteroid therapy, antiplatelet drugs, transfusions of plasma, splenectomy

Myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders

Chronic myelogenous leukemia

  • Clonal bone marrow stem cell disorder characterized by massive splenomegaly associated with proliferation of mature granulocytes, mostly neutrophils presenting Philadelphia chromosome
  • Asthenia, left upper quadrant pain, sweating, fever, weight loss
  • Bone pain, bleeding, extra-splenic myelogenous tumors
  • Splenectomy in hypersplenomegaly, repeated splenic infarction, hypersplenism
  • Chemo, radiotherapy

Myeloid metaplasia

  • Splenomegaly, bone marrow fibrosis, immature granulocytes
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, left upper quadrant pain, pallor (anemia), bleeding
  • Splenectomy

Malignant lymphoma

  • HL or NHL
  • Painful peripheral lymphadenopathy
  • Splenic metastasis
  • Night sweats, fever, itching, intensified by alcohol intake, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Splenectomy, chemo, radiotherapy

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

  • Accumulation of small lymphocytes in bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes and peripheral blood
  • Asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, fever, infectious complications, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly
  • Alkylating agents, corticotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, splenectomy

Hairy cell leukemia

  • Splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy and mononuclear cells with villi
  • Asthenia, fatigue, left upper quadrant pain, anemia, bleeding, infectious complications
  • Splenectomy

Splenic tumors

  • Benign tumors
    • Benign splenic cysts - hydatid cyst, primary cysts (serous cystadenoma, desmoid cyst, cystic hemangioma, cystic lymphangioma), secondary cysts (traumatic pseudocysts, degenerative necrotic cyst, inflammatory abscess)
    • Benign solid tumors – disembryoplasia (hamartoma), vascular hemangioma, lymphangioma, hemangiopericytoma
  • Cystic lesions comprise parasitic and nonparasitic cysts
  • Parasitic cysts are almost exclusively due to echinococcal disease
  • Non-parasitic cysts classified as primary (true) which have an epithelial lining or pseudocysts (more common)
  • Symptoms are vague and caused primarily by mass effect (compression of adjacent viscera)
  • Benign tumors treated surgically only if they become clinically active, with exception → hemangiomas (risk of rupture)
    • Flattening and filling of cyst, percutaneous puncture, aspiration and sclerotherapy in patients with definite diagnosis and high surgical risk
    • Aspiration, defenestration and electrocoagulation in case of superficial and uninfected cysts
    • Partial splenectomy in case of upper polar localization of tumors and small hemangiomas
    • Total splenectomy in case of large tumors with hilar location and suppurativecysts
  • Primary malignant tumors
    • Vascular structures: hemangiosarcoma, endothelial angiosarcoma, malignant hemangiopericytoma, lymphangiosarcoma
    • White pulp elements: brill-symmers disease (gigant follicular lymphoma), lymphosarcoma, plasmacytoma, reticulosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma
    • Capsule and trabeculae: fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma
  • Most common angiosarcomas
  • Symptoms - splenomegaly, malignant impregnation syndrome, pain in case of superinfection, tumor necrosis
  • Treatment - splenectomy +/- adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy
  • DD - splenomegaly and metastasis

Incidental splenectomy

  • Spleen is vulnerable to injury during operative procedures in upper abdomen
  • When splenic capsule is torn, splenectomy is frequently performed
  • Morbidity and mortality are higher with iatrogenic injury
Splenectomy
Absolute indicationsRelative indications
1. Splenic tumors
2. Metastatic disease
3. Splenic abscess
4. Pseudo-inflammatory tumors of spleen
5. Hereditary spherocytosis
6. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
7. Chronic myeloid leukemia
8. Sarcomas
9. Trauma
10. Benign tumors of the spleen
11. Hydatid cyst of spleen
12. Splenic vein thrombosis with ruptured gastric varices
13. Ruptured aneurysm		1. Congenital or autoimmune hemolytic anemias
2. Sickle cell anemia, thalassemia
3. Hereditary elliptocytosis
4. Thrombocytopenic purpura
5. Felty’s syndrome
6. Chronic rheumatoid arthritis
7. Splenic neutropenia
8. HL and NHL
9. Gaucher’s disease/Niemann-Pick disease
10. Leukemia
11. Myeloid metaplasia
12. Primary splenic pancreatitis
13. Cirrhosis with portal hypertension and
hypersplenism

Contraindications: myeloid leukemia, acute leukosis

  • Prior to removing spleen specific preoperative preparation necessary
  • All patients should receive polyvalent pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b

conjugant vaccine

  • Blood products should be available well in advance of surgery

Blood compositional changes in asplenic or hyposplenic patient

  • Absence of functional splenic tissue results in characteristic changes in circulating blood
  • Some of these are predictable and desirable results
  • These changes are considered measure of its success when splenectomy is performed for hematologic disease
  • Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) and thrombocytosis (desired result)
  • Other findings include target cells, acanthocytes, Heinz bodies and stippled red cells

Post-OP outcomes

  • 1. Siderocytes - red blood cells (erythrocyte) which contains iron granules
  • 2. Howell-Jolly bodies and thrombocytosis (desired result)
  • 3. Leukocytosis
  • 4. Increased platelet count

Complications

  • 1. Left lower lobe atelectasis = most common
  • 2. Subphrenic hematoma, bleeding
  • 3. Subphrenic abscess → can occur with placement of drain
  • 4. Pancreatitis → trauma to tail of pancreas
  • 5. Deep vein thrombosis → low dose anticoagulants
  • 6. Fulminant systemic sepsis with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus Pneumoniae, Neisseria Meningitidis,

HaemophilusInfluenzae

Hematological outcomes

Initiala. Thrombocytopenia → rise in platelet count within a few days
b. Chronic hemolytic anemias → Hgb level above 10 g/dl
Long terma. Increase in platelet count → rise to >150,000 more than 2 months after surgery
b. 90-100% success for hereditary spherocytosis

Immunological consequences

  • Causes slower and incomplete adaptive immune response against bacteria
  • Low levels of tuftsin, which stimulates phagocytosis by neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes
  • Decreased neutrophil and macrophage activity
  • Increased NK cell activity
  • Limited capacity of circulating B-cells to differentiate into antibody-secreting cells
  • Decreased level of T-cells

Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI)

  • 1. Lifetime risk of severe infection
  • 2. Incidence of 3.2% post-splenectomy
  • 3. Loss of the spleen’s ability to filter and phagocytose bacteria and infected RBC

Most common sources of infections

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae = most common
  • H. influenza
  • Meningococcus
  • Group A streptococci
  • Presents with pneumonia or meningitis

Prevention

  • Vaccine against
  • Pneumococcus
  • H. influenza
  • Meningococcus
  • to be given within 7-14 days after splenectomy

+ Booster dose for pneumococcal vaccine every 5-6 years

+ Annual H. influenza vaccine

+ Daily dose of penicillin or amoxicillin for 2 years

book.html:
The spleen

Lucian Mocan

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE SPLEEN:

The spleen is located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen, between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm, on the left side of thestomach. It has a reddish-brown color, measures about 12 cm and weighs 180-200 grams. It is coffee bean shaped, oval, with three sides, three edges and two extremities.

The surface of the spleen is covered by the peritoneum and further by the splenic capsule, which is a fibrous cover from which arise splenic trabeculae carrying arteries and veins. The splenic tissue is made of:

White pulp – approximately17-19% of the splenic parenchyma, consisting of lymphoreticular tissue;

Red pulp – 75-78% of the splenic parenchyma,consisting of reticular tissue, blood vessels and blood figurative elements;

Marginal zone – located between the white and the red pulp, with its own morphological structure and functions in immunological defense. It is the passage of B and T lymphocytes into the blood circulation.

Splenic vascularization - is ensured by the splenic artery (a branch of the celiac trunk), which enters the organ through the hilum, where it divides into 4-5 segmental trabecular arteries, and ends through arterial capillaries most open in the red pulp venous sinuses, the remaining opening directly into the reticular tissue. The venous system of the spleen begins with the venous sinuses, venous blood is carried into pulp trabecular veins and flows through the splenic vein into the portal vein. Spleen blood flow is approximately 10 l/h.

Innervation of the spleen is achieved by sympathetic nerve fibers coming from the celiac plexus and through the branches of the left vagus nerve.

FUNCTIONS OF THE SPLEEN

1. The hematopoietic function: the spleen plays an important role in lymphoid hematopoiesis, but this is not its primary site.

2. The filtering function: the spleen phagocytes damaged or aged erythrocytes, germs, antigens and cellular debris. About 70% of platelets are also destroyed in the spleen, at the end of their life. The removal of certain inclusions (Howell-Jolly bodies, Heinz bodies) from viable red blood cells to reintroduce cells into the blood flow is exclusively splenic. Pathologically, the spleen phagocytes imperfect erythrocytes by volume or shape defects (spherocytosis), through the abnormal hemoglobin content (hemoglobinopathy), prolonged stagnation (portal hypertension, hemolytic anemia, myeloproliferativeand lymphoproliferativedisorders) or those loaded with IgG (autoimmune anemia).

3. The storage function: under normal conditions, the spleen houses platelets (40% of the total weight), granulocytes (50% of the total weight), monocytes and lymphocytes (75% B cells and 25% Tcells).

4. The circulatory function: provides aortic and portal blood flowdynamics. The importance of this function is shown in cases of portal hypertension, when there is a great increase in trans-splenicblood flow.

5. The immunological function: phagocytosis, humoral and cellmediated immune response, immunological information transmission. The spleen has an important role in infections –it extracts antigens from the blood flow and produceslymphokines and antibodies activating the complement system (achievable both in the red pulp and white pulp).

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND SPLENOPATHY

1. Hypersplenism:

Hypersplenism is a condition that causes an exacerbation of normal splenic function translated into an increase in the damage of figurative elements of blood with altered hematopoiesis. Hypersplenism is often associated with splenomegaly, and splenectomy usually provides a favorable clinical response. Hypersplenism is due to several reasons:

Autoimmune diseases that generate autoantibodies or structural damage of blood cells, splenic stasis with cellular impairment,local factors that alter hematogenousbone marrow.

Hypersplenism causes can be divided into two major categories: primary and secondary.

  • Primary hypersplenism
  • Congenital hemolytic anemia - hereditary microspherocytosis, elliptocytosis, poikilocytosis, beta thalassaemia
  • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (Werlhof’s disease)
  • Splenic neutropenia of Wieseman and Doan
  • Immune hemolytic anemia.
  • Secondary hypersplenism
  • Lymphoma: Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Chronic bacterial infections: tuberculosis, syphilis
  • Portal hypertension
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis
  • Thesaurismosis: Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease
  • Chronic leukemia: lymphocytic leukemia, myeloid leukemia, hairy cell leukemia.

2. Hyposplenism and asplenia

Hyposplenism is characterized by decreased splenic functioning due to splenic tissue loss. Hyposplenism can have multiple causes, from extensive vascular damage, surgical interventions, or tissue replacement.

Asplenia refers to the complete absence of splenic function. It can be congenital or it might occur after splenectomy, splenic irradiation,or repeated splenic infarctions.

The two pathologies expose the body to severe infections by reducing opsonin production, phagocytosis and the production of IgG and IgM antibodies.

CLINICAL AND PARACLINICAL DATA TO DIAGNOSE SPLEEN

DISORDERS

Medical history: patients’ medical history can sometimes help identify bleeding disorders, anemic syndromes, recurrent infections, abdominal trauma, or sometimes patients had already been diagnosed.

Symptoms of patients with splenic disease are minimal. There may be discomfort or left upper quadrant pain, with or without being referred to the left shoulder (violent pain can be attributed to splenic infarction or abscess). The occurrence of jaundice with acholic stools, coluric urine and lack of itching may indicate hemolytic jaundice.

Physical examination:

  • Palpation: examination should be performed during deep inspiration,

with the patient in the supine or right lateral position, with the examiner’s hand placed under the left costal margin. The specific evidence (to distinguish the spleen from other intra-abdominal tumor masses) is given by the crenulated appearanceand the movement mobility during inspiration and expiration. Under normal conditions, the spleen is rarely palpable, only in asthenic patients (in approximately 2% of the cases); palpation is clinically useful in case of splenomegaly. Splenomegaly can vary and the spleen can sometimes becomevery enlarged (massive splenomegaly), when it can be observed during the examination. In such cases, the crenulated appearance can be observed on the anterior edge of the spleen.

  • Percussion reveals dullness in case of splenomegaly.

The differential diagnosis of splenomegaly is arrived at when there are tumors in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen: •abdominal wall tumors,

  • retroperitoneal sarcomas, •left adrenal tumors, •left kidney tumors, •left

hydronephrosis, •cancer of the tail of the pancreas, •cancer of the greater curvature, •giant tumors in the vicinity or •hypertrophy of the left hepatic lobe.

Paraclinical data:

Imaging evaluation

  • Abdominal ultrasound examination very important when

establishing the differential diagnosis (not to be confused with other

diseases: tumors of the left splenic flexure, left kidney tumors). Indirect

radiological signs of splenopathy are given by increased splenic shadow,

elevated left phrenic dome, changes in stomach appearance.Abdominal

ultrasound is the method of choice available in the hospital ward. It is a

fast and repetitive technique. It has up to 90% accuracy in measuring the

size of the spleen, observing collections, hematoma or splenic tumors,

splenic ruptures, being able toestablish the differential diagnosis,

distinguishing it from other abdominal tumors. Doppler ultrasound can

also provide information on splenic vascularization, being extremely

useful in traumatic emergencies.

  • Computed tomography (CT) provides high quality additional

information on tumor and traumatic spleen pathologies. It is indicated

when abdominal ultrasound is inconclusive or for monitoring the evolution of pathological processes (intrasplenic and perisplenic hematoma);

  • Radioisotope examination: splenic scintigraphy with 99mTc-

sulphate or labeling erythrocytes with 51Cr are two of the methods commonly used in the past to assess splenoportal axis, but after the introduction of abdominal ultrasound and CT scan they no longer find use in the diagnosis of spleen disorders;

  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is less useful in the diagnosis

of splenic lesions. In selected cases it helps differentiate between benign tumors from malignant tumors.

Laboratory examination

  • Blood cytology is mandatory in order to assess peripheral

cytopenia: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, anemia;

  • Blood cytology in the bone marrow (sternal puncture) is done to

assess the regenerative potential of bone marrow in case of hypersplenism.

Immunological examinations: direct and indirect Coombs test, autoantibody tests.

Indications for splenectomy

Indications for splenectomy are classified into therapeutic, diagnostic and tactical indications. Therapeutic indications are classified into relative and absolute. 1. Relative indications for splenectomy

  • autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • congenital hemolytic anemia
  • splenic neutropenia
  • splenic pancytopenia
  • sickle cell disease, thalassemia
  • thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  • immune thrombocytopenic purpura
  • Felty's syndrome
  • pyruvate kinase deficiency
  • myeloid metaplasia
  • chronic lymphocytic leukemia;
  • chronicmyelogenous leukemia
  • hairy cell leukemia
  • primary splenic pancreatitis
  • hereditaryelliptocytosis
  • follicular lymphoma (Brill-Symmers disease)
  • Gaucher’s disease
  • Niemann-Pick disease
  • cirrhosis with portal hypertension and hypersplenism (after

portacaval shunting)

2. Absolute indications for splenectomy

  • benign tumors of the spleen
  • pseudo-inflammatory tumors of the spleen
  • hereditary spherocytosis
  • tumorsof the spleen
  • trauma
  • hydatid cyst of the spleen
  • splenic abscess
  • ruptured aneurysm
  • splenic vein thrombosis with ruptured gastric varices

3. Diagnostic indications for splenectomy

  • tumors of the spleen with an undefined etiology
  • lymphomas

4.Tactical indications for splenectomy

  • totalgastrectomy
  • corporeo-caudal pancreatectomy
  • lefthemicolectomy
  • left nephrectomy

5. Contraindications for splenectomy

  • myeloid leukemia
  • acuteleukosis

Postoperative changes in blood cytology may occur: transient polycythemia, Howell-Jolly bodies in the blood flow (punctate basophilia, representing nuclear DNA remnants), Heinz bodies (small round bluish inclusions at the periphery of the cell), reticulocytes (young immature anucleate erythrocytescontaining residual nucleic acids), "target" red blood cells,transient hyperleukocytosis, thrombocytosis (the most common). There might be immunological changes leading to sometimes fatal septicemia (especially in children).

Complications of splenectomy do not always occur, but when they do, they are represented by: 5-6% bleeding, half of these cases requiring another surgical intervention; 2-4% acute pancreatitis, which can occur asresponse to direct trauma, stopped blood circulationbysectioning of the pancreatic vessels; 10% thromboembolic complications, which generally occur in the absence of thromboprophylaxis and they are mainly due to hypercoagulability generated by consequent thrombocytosis; 1-5% fulminant systemic sepsis, caused by contamination with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus Pneumoniae, Neisseria Meningitidis, HaemophilusInfluenzae.

Splenic injury

Splenic tissue friability and anatomy turn the spleen intoone of the parenchymal organs that is most affected by abdominal trauma (30-35% of all closed abdominal trauma). Frequently, these lesions occurwithin splenic pathological processes (enlarged spleen), making the spleen even morevulnerable.

Causes:

  • spleen contusion, ruptured spleen
  • immediate rupture (most commonly pathological splenic rupture);
  • delayed splenic rupture
  • penetrating wounds (produced with cold weapons or firearms);
  • iatrogenic injury (intra-operatory injury - during colon, stomach and

pancreatic surgery).

Morphology :

The immediate consequence of spleen injury is bleeding, which may be either limited (hematoma) or can cause haemoperitoneum.

  • Subcapsular splenic hematoma occurs after closed trauma with

preserved capsule integrity. It may evolve towardssecondary capsule

rupture and delayed hemorrhage, seclusion, abscess or resorption.

  • Perisplenic hematoma occurs by capsular effraction, trauma or

secondary to the development of a subcapsular hematoma. It requires

careful monitoring of the patient when considering the conservative

treatment. It may evolve towards secondary rupture (hemoperitoneum)

or seclusion.

  • Splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum (mainly occurs on the convex

side of the spleen) is the most common and it can be fatal. Splenic pedicle

avulsion is very rare but extremely serious and requires emergency

laparotomy. It occurs in case of strong trauma which causes splenic hilum

compressionagainst the backbone.

  • Wounds produced by cold weapons usually avoid thesplenic hilum.

They are linear and can differ in depth and shape (linear, simple,

stellate,of variable depth). They may be associated or not with the

detachment of parenchymal fragments. Firearm wounds are complex and

can sometimes lead to splenic parenchymal fragmentation (in serious

situations they determine the so-called "spleen explosion").

Clinical diagnosis:

There are various clinical manifestations, depending on injury severity, associated lesions, time from the occurrence of trauma.

Hypovolemic shock is one of the main events occurring duringintraperitoneal hemorrhage (75% of cases): anxiety, thirst, faintness, severe skin paleness, cold and wet hands and feet, hypotension, peripheral impingement, oliguria. Sudden onset of hypovolemic shock is a sign of massive bleeding, requiring emergency laparotomy. In these cases, the diagnosis is established based on patient history.

Local signs are represented by the sudden left upper quadrant pain with or without being referred to the left shoulder, tenderness on palpating the left upper quadrant with or without signs of peritoneal irritation, superficial thrombophlebitis.

Hemoperitoneum is manifested by abdominal distension, movable dullness (Ballance’s sign), paralytic ileus, bulging of the Pouch of Douglas.

Paraclinicaldata

Laboratory examinations detect anemia, leukocytosis (80% of cases) and/or thrombocytosis.

As an imaging exam (after volemicrebalancing), abdominal ultrasound reveals splenic hematoma or hemoperitoneum. CT scan can provide additional data, but is not indicated for massive bleeding.

Treatment

Regaining vital functions (volemicrebalancing, cardiopulmonary resuscitation) is the first step that needs to be taken. Depending on injury severity,surgery is or is not the method of choice.

Non-surgical spleen preservation treatment is possible in carefully selected cases: hemodynamically stable patients, splenic injury without active bleeding, absence of associated lesions. Due to possibledelayedrupture in these patients, hospitalization for a period of at least 6-8 days with continuous clinical monitoring and imaging is recommended.

Spleen-preservingsurgery (capsular suture, tissue adhesives, argon plasma coagulation) prevents serious infections after splenectomy. The decision for spleen preservation is made intraoperativelytaking into account the degree of parenchymal injury, surgeon experience and available technology.

Complete splenectomy is performed in case of total spleen damage or in case of splenic bleeding that cannot be stopped by means of splenic preservation treatment.

INFECTIOUS AND PARASITIC SPLENIC DISEASES

Splenic abscess

Abscesses are rare purulent collections (<1%) caused by bacteria or fungi.

Causes

1. Overinfectedintrasplenic hematoma,

hematogeniccontamination of splenic infarction, overinfected

necrotic lesion.

2. Hematogenic propagation from a primary extrasplenicseptic

focus: bacterial endocarditis, lung abscess, osteomyelitis, typhoid

fever, etc.

3. Lymphatic propagation from the neighboring organs:

pancreatic suppuration,overinfected left colic tumors.

The diagnosis is suspected in patients with systemic infections, multiple traumaor immunosuppressed showing sudden occurrence of left upper quadrant pain, tenderness during palpation, superficial thrombophlebitis, fever, malaise.

Laboratory tests reveal leukocytosis, positive blood cultures.

Ultrasound scan is the imaging exam of choice, detecting an irregular hypoechoicimage, with echoes on the inside. CT scan confirms the presence of splenic abscess and can detect the presence of small abscesses.

Treatment

Antibiotherapy associated with surgery is compulsory in these patients. Splenectomy is primary, but ultrasound-guided percutaneous abscess evacuation and drainage can be performed in case of single abscesses.

Splenic hydatid cyst

Location in the spleen is third in terms of frequency (2-3% in endemic areas), after lungs and liver. To reach the spleen, the hexacanth embryo must go through lung and liver filters, being an arterial inflammation. The cyst may be single or multiple, varying in diameter, with clear or purulent content. Throughout its evolution, it may protrude on one of the spleen sides leading to compression of neighboring organs. It can cause perisplenitis, adhering to neighboring organs, it may result in splenic rupture (freely into the peritoneal cavityor sectional, it may perforate the neighboring organs, it can penetrate the pleura or bronchitransdiaphragmatically) or it can lead to splenic calcification (rare).

Clinical diagnosis for uncomplicated hydatidcyst is extremely rare, as during palpationonly splenomegalycan be detected. In case of complications, there are systemic symptoms: the free rupture into the peritoneal cavity produces anaphylactic shock,abcedation will result insuppurative collections of the splenic abscess. Ultrasound-based diagnosis is confirmed by positive serological tests: Casoni test, indirect hemagglutination test, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

Surgical treatment of splenic hydatid cyst, based on the location and extent of the cyst, consists in: partial cyst resection or partial splenectomy (after evacuation by aspiration and inactivation with scolicidal agents) or total splenectomy.

Splenic tumors

1. Benign tumors are classified into:

  • Benign splenic cysts
  • hydatid cyst
  • primary cysts: serous cystadenoma, epithelial cyst (desmoid cyst,

epidermoid cyst), endothelial cyst (cystic hemangioma, cystic

lymphangioma)

  • secondary cysts: traumatic cyst (pseudocysts), degenerative cyst

(necrotic cyst), inflammatory cyst (abscess)

  • Benign solid tumors
  • disembryoplasia: hamartoma
  • vascularhemangioma, lymphangioma, hemangiopericytoma
  • other tumors: lipoma, fibroma, chondroma, osteoma, leiomyoma

Benign tumors are treated surgically only if they become clinically active, with an exception from this rule forhemangiomas, due to the risk of rupture. Depending on tumor location and progression, the following procedures can be performed:

  • flattening and filling of theepiploon, percutaneous puncture, aspiration and sclerotherapy in patients with definite diagnosis and high surgical risk
  • aspiration, defenestration and electrocoagulation in case of superficial and uninfected cysts
  • partial splenectomy in case of upper polar localization of tumors and small hemangiomas
  • total splenectomy is the method of choice in case of large tumors with hilar location and suppurativecysts

2. Primary malignant tumors are rare and appear in:

  • vascular structures: hemangiosarcoma, endothelial angiosarcoma, malignant hemangiopericytoma, lymphangiosarcoma
  • white pulp elements: Brill-Symmers disease (gigantofollicularlymphoma), lymphosarcoma, plasmacytoma
  • whitepulp: reticulosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma
  • capsule and trabeculae: fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma

Diagnosis: symptoms are dominated by splenomegaly,malignant impregnation syndrome. Pain appears in case of superinfection, tumor necrosis.

Treatment consists of splenectomy and it is an absolute indication which can be associated with adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

HAEMATOLOGICAL DISORDERS

Hereditary spherocytosis

(Congenital hemolytic jaundice or Minkowski-Chauffard disease)

Hereditary disease with an autosomal dominant trait,hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by increased osmotic fragility of erythrocytes, anemia, acholuricjaundice, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones.

Characteristics

  • Red blood cell membrane defectsresulting inreduced surface and

spherocyte. This ishighly exposed to intrasplenic hemolysis.

  • Thick and rigid membrane, preventing adequate erythrocyte

deformability, not being able to cross interendothelial holes, thus being retained in the red pulp cords and destroyed by the reticuloendothelial system.

Diagnosis

  • sclero-tegumentary jaundice occurring in spurts, without itching skin and always acholuric;
  • intermittent anemia associatedwith asthenia;
  • constant splenomegaly that can become massive, leading to compression phenomena;
  • hemolytic crises (impaired general condition, tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain) occur for no apparent reason or may be triggered by infection or physical effort.

Laboratory tests reveal anemia, reticulocytosis, the presence of microspherocytes with increased osmotic fragility, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, increased fecal excretion of urobilinogen, Coomb's negative reaction.

Imaging exams

  • skull radiographs may detectthe "tower-like" skull (thickening of frontal and parietal bones); heterotopic tumors of the bone marrow (spinal tumors);
  • abdominal ultrasound detects splenomegaly and possible accessory spleen.

Treatment consists of splenectomy. The optimal time for such an intervention is after the age of 6 years. Thus, jaundice and anemia are resolved. Failure occurs when accessory spleens are not discovered intraoperatively.

Splenic neutropenia

(Doan-Wiseman disorder)

It is a rare condition characterized by splenomegaly, peripheral neutropenia and normal or hyperplastic bone marrow.

Characteristics: histiocytic predominance of phagocytic granulocytes in the spleen, suggesting excessive intraspleniclysis.

Left upper quadrant pain, splenomegaly and recurrent infections are some of the clinical manifestations of splenic neutropenia.

Treatment consists of splenectomy, with clinical improvement in most cases. Relapses are extremely rare.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

(Werlhof’s disease)

The disease mainly affects young women without medical history. Sometimes, it can occur in systemic diseases that disrupt immune mechanisms: systemic lupus erythematosus, Hodgkin's disease, AIDS, etc.

It is characterized by hemorrhagiparous syndrome,peripheral thrombocytopenia,bone marrowmegakaryocytes, the presence of antiplatelet antibodies in patient serum.

The insidious clinical onset manifests through the appearance of petechiaeon slopeor compression areas (bone prominences), gingival bleeding and epistaxis, bruising, uterine bleeding, hematuria, intracranial haemorrhage.

The spleen is usually normal sized, splenomegaly being observed in only 2% of patients.

Diagnosis is based on hematologic examination which detects prolonged bleeding time andperipheral thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow puncture shows an increase in megakaryocytes.Positive Rumpel-Leede test.

Treatment is indicated for patients with spontaneous bleeding. Initially,corticotherapy is tested (approx. 75% of cases). Splenectomy is indicated in patients who do not respond favorably to cortisone administration, in those with frequent relapseand in patients with risk of bleeding.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

It is a rapidly progressive disease, with a severe prognosis when there is no treatment and with an unclear etiology. Peak incidence is in women in the third decade of life. Pathologically, there are disseminated obstructions in arterioles and capillaries caused by endoluminalstorage of platelet microthrombi.

Clinical manifestations are represented by hemolytic anemia and jaundice, generalized purpura,menometroragy, neurospihic syndrome (aphasia, hemiparesis, delirium, seizures).

Laboratory tests detect anemia with reticulocytosis, moderate leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, decreased prothrombin time, abnormal kidney function test, proteinuria, hematuria and azotemia.

Treatment consists in high-dose corticosteroid therapy, antiplatelet drugs, transfusions of fresh frozen plasma. Splenectomy is indicated when conservative treatmentdoes not result in remission, but it is not a cure.

Hereditary elliptocytosis

It is a hereditary disorder with autosomal dominant transmission characterized by the presence of ovalocytes, erythrocyte cell membrane abnormality giving them the oval shape.

Clinically, hemolysis and splenomegaly are present. Most patients are asymptomatic, splenectomy being indicated in patients with severe hemolysis.

Sickle-cell disease

The disease is characterized by the presence of “sickle-shaped” red blood cellscontaining HgS, an abnormalsickle-cell hemoglobin.

Clinically, it occurs as painful hemolytic crisis and vascular occlusive events.

Splenectomy is necessary due to the high risk of splenic infarction.

Thalassemia

It is a congenital anemia characterized by deficient synthesis of one or more hemoglobin polypeptide chains.

It has a homozygous form called thalassemia major (due to the severity of the disease) and a heterozygous form, thalassemia minor.

Thalassemia major occurs in the first year of life by progressive anemia, hemolytic jaundice, splenomegaly, delayedbone growth and bone loss.

Hematological aspects: hypochromic anemia, microcytic anemia, presence of “target-shaped” red blood cells, indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

Splenectomy results in clinical andhematologic improvement, but does not influence the hematologic abnormality.

Other types of congenital hemolytic anemia

Hydrocytosis, hereditary xerocytosis, dyserytropoietic anemia, enzymedeficient anemia, erythropoietic porphyria are among the types of hemolytic anemia where splenectomy can improve anemia and decrease the need for transfusion.

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

The disease is caused by abnormal production of antibodies in oppostionto the body’s own red blood cells. Splenic macrophages and Kupffer cells capture erythrocytes that are attached to autoantibodies and phagocyte them or turn them into spherocytes.

Onset is usually after the age of 40 years, when chronic hemolytic anemia, fluctuating jaundice and splenomegaly occur.

Hematological aspects: anemia, the presence of spherocytes and microspherocytes, reticulocytosis and erythroid hyperplasia. Red blood cells have short lifespan.

Treatment consists of immunosuppressive medication and blood transfusion, and patients who do not respond favorably are candidates for splenectomy.

Felty's Syndrome

It occurs as a complication in advanced-stage rheumatoid arthritis. It is characterized by rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly and neutropenia, predisposing the body to severe and recurrent bacterial infections. Splenectomy improves granulocytopenia and decreases the risk of recurrent infections.

LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASES

Gaucher’s disease

It is a rare inherited disorder, a so called autosomal recessive disorder. It is characterized by the accumulation of glucocerebroside in the monocytophagocytic system in the spleen, liver, lung and bone marrow. Clinically, it isaccompanied by massive splenomegaly with hypersplenism, possible hepatomegaly with hepatic fibrosis, leading to portal hypertension with esophageal varices, cutaneous hyperpigmentation of areas exposed to the sun, yellow coloring of the cornea and conjunctiva, inexplicable recurrent infections, bone lesions.

Gaucher’s disease has three common clinical subtypes:

  • thechronic type - the most common, occurring in adults;
  • the acute type - neurological symptoms and death, it occurs in infants;
  • thesubacute type - attenuated neurological manifestations, favorable

prognosis.

Splenectomy does not cure the disease but remits symptoms and corrects blood cytopenia. In association with bone marrow transplantation, it leads to progressive decrease inGauchercells in bone marrow.

Niemann-Pick disease

It is an inherited disorder, a so called autosomal recessive disorder. It is caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency, resulting in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in macrophages in the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, central nervous system and bone marrow.

Niemann-Pick cells are large cells with 1-2 nuclei and honeycombpattern cytoplasm.

Clinical manifestations are dominated in hepatosplenomegaly. There are three main types of Niemann-Pick disease:

  • TypeA, infantile form,has its onset during childhood and

presentsspleno-hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy and mental retardation

  • Type B begins in childhood, without signs of central nervous system

involvement

  • Type C has its onset after the age of 2 years and progresses to death

Splenectomy is performed to reduce symptoms, but it does not influence disease progression.

MYELOPROLIFERATIVE DISEASES

Chronic myelogenous leukemia

It is a clonal bone marrow stem cell disorder characterized bymassive splenomegaly associated with proliferation of mature granulocytes, mostly neutrophils presenting the Philadelphia chromosome (chromosome abnormality present in 95% of patients).

The onset is mainly in the 4th and 5th decade of life and it is seen as an inherited disorder. The disease evolves in two phases:

  • The chronic phase, with accumulation of granulocytes and precursors in the blood and bone marrow, with a certain ratio between mature and immature forms;
  • The blast phase, with an increase in the proportion of blasts and promyelocytes in the blood and bone marrow.

Clinical onset begins with asthenia, left upper quadrant pain, sweating, fever, weight loss. Disease progression is characterized by the presence of bone pain, bleeding complications, extrasplenicmyelogenoustumors.

Diagnosis is mainly established as a result of laboratory tests. The hematologic aspectis given by hyperleukocytosis, normochromic and normocytic anemia, increase in absolute basophil, eosinophil and monocyte count. Blood serum reveals an increase in vitamin B12, uric acid, LDH and potassium. Bone marrow biopsydetects the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome.

The treatment is conservative: chemotherapy and radiotherapy in combination with bone marrow transplantation. In the chronic phase,alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, busulfan, melphalan) and hydroxyurea can be administered. In the blast phase, patients may benefit from the administration of vincristine and prednisone in addition tohydroxyurea. Splenectomy is indicated in patients with hypersplenomegaly, repeated splenic infarctionand pronounced hypersplenism.

Myeloid metaplasia

It is a rare disease of unknown etiology, characterized by splenomegaly, bone marrow fibrosis and appearance of immature granulocytes, teardropshaped erythrocytes and red blood cells in the blood.

Clinical manifestations are represented byhepatosplenomegaly, left upper quadrant pain, pallor (syndrome of anemia), bleeding syndrome.

Splenectomy is performed in patients with refractory thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anemia during the conservative treatment. It brings haematologicalimprovement and improves quality of life.

LYMPHOPROLIFERATIVE DISORDERS

Malignant lymphoma

1. Hodgkin's lymphoma is characterized by the presence of mononucleated Hodgkin cells and giant multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells.

There are four histologic subtypes:

  • lymphocyte-rich HL
  • nodularsclerosing HL
  • mixed cellularity HL
  • lymphocyte depletedHL

Onset is marked by painful peripheral lymphadenopathy, especially laterocervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Metastasis includes the deep lymphatic territory. At the time of diagnosis, 40-76% of patients also present splenic metastasis.

Systemic symptoms occur in advanced HL stages and include night sweats, fever, itching, which is intensified by alcohol intake, weight loss, abdominal pain and vomiting.

The diagnosis is established based on paraclinicaldata: abdominal ultrasound, CT, histopathologic examination of lymph node biopsy, diagnostic laparoscopy.

Treatment of Hodgkin’s lymphoma is based on chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Splenectomy is indicated for the correction of peripheral cytopenia.

2.Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are a group of malignant neoplasms of lymphoreticular tissue.

Histological classification

  • well-differentiated lymphocytic lymphoma
  • poorly differentiated lymphocytic lymphoma
  • undifferentiatedlymphociticlymphoma
  • lymphohistiocytic lymphoma
  • follicular lymphoma

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can start anywhere in the body, without any favorite organ.

If the onset is in the spleen, splenomegaly occurs with or withouthypersplenism. Systemic symptoms occur in case of disseminated diseases with poor prognosis.

Basic treatment consists of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, while splenectomy is a palliative procedure.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

It is the most frequent type of leukemia, characterized by the accumulation of small lymphocytes in the bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes and peripheral blood.

Etiopathogenetically, there are two subtypes:

  • clonal proliferation of neoplastic B lymphocytes, >95% of cases, progressing with hypogammaglobulinemia
  • clonal proliferation of T lymphocytes, 2-5% of cases Clinical manifestations: asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, fever,

infectious complications, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.

Diagnosis is established based on laboratory exams which detect: peripheral lymphocytosis, anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia.

Leukemia staging

  • Stage A -lymphocytosis involvingless than three lymph node areas
  • Stage B - lymphocytosis involving more than three lymph node areas
  • Stage C - anemia and thrombocytopenia, regardless of the number of lymph node areas affected

Treatment is conservative and consists of therapy with alkylating agents; corticotherapy in case of autoimmune hemolytic anemia; polychemotherapy in advanced stages; radiotherapy in localized disease forms; immunotherapy in case of associatedhypogammaglobulinemia; splenectomy in patients with hypersplenismand refractory to other therapies, in patients with symptomatic splenomegaly and in those withchlorambucil-resistant leukemia (therapy carried out for 6 months).

Hairy cell leukemia

It is a rare type of leukemia that mainly occurs in middle-aged men. It is characterized by the appearance of splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy and mononuclear cells with cytoplasmic villi and flagellated aspect (hairy cells).

Clinical manifestations: asthenia, fatigue, left upper quadrant pain, anemia, bleeding, infectious complications.

Hematologic manifestations: pancytopenia, hairy cells (in peripheral blood and bone marrow).

Splenectomy is indicated in patients with significant peripheral cytopenia, massive splenomegaly, focal bone marrow infiltration with hairy cells.

VASCULAR SPLENOPATHY

Splenic artery aneurysm

Splenic artery aneurysm occurs more frequently in women and it is the thirdmost common abdominal aneurysm,after aortic and iliacartery aneurysms.

The cause may be atheromatous, destructionof the tunica media, trauma, syphilis, pancreatitis or malformative.

Most aneurysms are asymptomatic. Symptoms of disease onset might be indicated by left upper quadrant pain, sometimesreferred into the left subscapular area, exacerbated by physical effort. In 15% of cases it begins with rupture and signs of hypovolemic shock.

Radiologic examinations can detect calcified splenic artery and the diagnosis can be supported by Doppler ultrasound or selective angiography.

Treatment consists of emergency surgery, performed based on the location of the aneurysm: aneurysmal sac resection and splenic artery ligation

  • spleen vascularizationbeing supplied throughthe short gastric arteries,

resections with vascular prosthesis or vascular anastomosis, splenectomy for aneurysms located in the hilum, splenopancreatectomy for aneurysms in the retropancreatic region.

Splenic arteriovenous fistulas

Splenic arteriovenous fistulas may be associated with aneurysmsand may occur after trauma or splenectomy. They may occur during the evolution of inflammatory pancreatic diseases. Symptoms includecolicky abdominal pain, splenomegaly, portal hypertension (hyperinflux), heavy breath in the spleen area during auscultation. The diagnosis is established by means of selective arteriography.

Treatment consists of vein ligation and resection of arteriovenouscommunication in disease forms occurring after splenectomy, vessel separation and vascular defect repair, or splenectomy.

Splenic vein thrombosis

It can be caused by acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, pseudocysts, neoplasms, trauma, splenic vein abnormalities, other conditions that predispose to thrombophlebitis.

The diagnosis should be suspected in patients presenting splenomegaly and gastroesophageal varices without hepatic damage, and it is established by means of Eco-Doppler or selective angiography.

Treatment consists of splenectomy in most cases.

Splenic infarction

Causes

  • embolic diseases: valvular heart disease, endocarditis, myocardial infarction, aneurysms
  • systemic diseases: sickle-cell anemia, chronic myelogenous leukemia, polycythemia vera, lymphomas, osteomyelofibrosis, polyarteritisnodosa, sepsis

Disease progressionis characterized by futurepseudocysts, abscess, retractile fibrosis. The diagnosis can be established by means of ultrasound or angiography.

Splenectomy is indicated in case of complications.
